source: Wallas (1926) The Art of Thought
finding: Wallas names four stages by dissecting one achievement of thought, taking Helmholtz's 1891 banquet speech as the template: Preparation, Incubation, Illumination. He adds Verification himself.
numbers: Four stages. Helmholtz gave three; Wallas added Verification. Poincare's two mathematical discoveries are the second worked case: hard fruitless preparation, then a break (military service; a journey), then a sudden idea, then verification.
quote: Helmholtz: ideas 'come unexpectedly without effort' and never when 'my mind was fatigued'
limits: Built from anecdotes by famous thinkers (Helmholtz, Poincare), not experiments. Wallas says the stages overlap in the stream of thought. No effect size exists in the book.
agent_relevance: Stages are a description of a human process, not a recipe. Use them as labels for states, but evidence for each stage's causal role must come from later experiments.

source: Wallas (1926) The Art of Thought
finding: Wallas splits Incubation into two forms: spending the break on other problems, or relaxing from all conscious work. He says the first saves time, but hard creative work needs real relaxation.
numbers: Two forms. Example: a preacher who posed his sermon problem on Monday got a better sermon than posing it late in the week, with the same hours of work. Wallas notes barristers deliberately delay each brief.
limits: Anecdote and opinion. The sermon case is an N=1 report with no control. The 'relaxation' claim is what Sio and Ormerod (2009) later found false for linguistic problems.
agent_relevance: Wallas already allows that the break can be a different task rather than idleness. For our agent, 'work on a different subtask' is the cheap analog of incubation; 'idle' is not.

source: Wallas (1926) The Art of Thought
finding: Wallas adds a sub-stage of Illumination called Intimation: a fringe-conscious feeling that the flash is coming. He advises thinkers to notice it and protect it from interruption.
numbers: Chapter synopsis: Intimation is part of the Illumination stage. Verification uses conscious rules like Preparation.
quote: Intimation: fringe-conscious events that 'precede and accompany the flash of Illumination'
limits: Introspective. Intimation is rarely tested directly; Gilhooly (2016) says it is often overlooked.
agent_relevance: An agent could log a cheap 'warmth' signal (partial-solution confidence) before an answer appears. Untested for LLMs; do not treat as validated.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 135, 94-120)
finding: The best meta-analysis of incubation finds a real but small-to-medium positive effect, with wide spread between studies and mostly small samples.
numbers: 117 studies, 3,606 participants, median 25 per study. 85 of 117 effect sizes positive. Unweighted mean unbiased d = 0.41 (SD 0.71, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.54); median d = 0.26. Outliers beyond 2 SD recoded.
limits: Small studies (median N=25). Outliers recoded. Different tasks pooled. Heterogeneity was significant, so one number hides large variation. Later reviews quote a weighted mean near d = 0.29.
agent_relevance: Incubation help is plausible but not large and not reliable per study: 32 of 117 studies had a zero or negative effect. Do not make it a default step.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 135, 94-120)
finding: Publication bias looked absent in the funnel-plot regression, but the test is weak with small studies.
numbers: Regression of weighted effect size on sample size: standardized beta = .08, p = .41 (no sign of bias). Cochran Q heterogeneity significant, so random-effects model used.
limits: Funnel tests are weak at this scale. Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) found strong funnel asymmetry in the related unconscious-thought literature, so absence here is not proof.
agent_relevance: Treat the 0.3 to 0.4 range as an upper estimate.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 135, 94-120)
finding: Moderators: divergent (creative) tasks gain more than visual and linguistic insight tasks; a longer preparation period gives a larger effect; a high-demand filler task gives a smaller effect.
numbers: Visual and linguistic insight effects each smaller than creative-problem effects (visual vs linguistic z = 1.25, n.s.). Preparation length coefficient significant (p<.05). Preparation length vs effect: visual r(35)=.40, p=.02; creative r(14)=.60, p=.03; linguistic r(65)=.04, p=.75. Table 4 weighted means as extracted from PDF text: low-load filler 0.52, rest 0.46, high-load filler 0.24 (check table layout).
limits: Correlational across studies, not randomized. Only 14 creative-problem studies and 16 rest studies. Table columns were garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Incubation pays most after real prior effort. A 'step away' operator should fire only after a serious failed attempt (matches guardrail G1).

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 135, 94-120)
finding: Surprise result: for linguistic insight problems, a low-demand filler task beat pure rest. Rest was not the best incubation.
numbers: Within linguistic problems, low-load task vs rest: beta = .54, p < .05. The task-type interaction held only for linguistic problems; no such difference for visual problems.
limits: Number of rest-only studies was small (16). Sio and Ormerod read it as covert work or spreading activation rather than recovery.
agent_relevance: The LLM analog of 'rest' (no tokens) is empty. A light unrelated task is the only meaningful analog, and a stateless model has no process that continues during it.

source: Dodds, Ward & Smith (2003) review of incubation experiments, as reported in Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014)
finding: Early qualitative review: most lab experiments found incubation effects, with a few clear failures.
numbers: Dodds et al. reviewed 39 experiments; 29 of 39 found a significant incubation effect. Olton and Johnson (1976) found no effect. A clue given during incubation helps if useful and hurts if misleading.
limits: Secondary report. Vote counting of significance, not effect size.
agent_relevance: Cues in the break can help or hurt: any background context during a reframe step must be curated.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Four rival explanations for incubation: intermittent conscious work, beneficial forgetting (including Segal's Fresh Look), unconscious work, and recovery from fatigue.
numbers: Delayed incubation (break after work) vs immediate incubation (break before work). Sio and Ormerod mean d about 0.29 over 117 studies; Strick et al. (2011) g = 0.224 over 92 decision studies for immediate incubation.
quote: Wallas proposed 'spreading associative chains' active during incubation, anticipating spreading-activation ideas
limits: Reviewer favours unconscious work; weigh accordingly. The theories make different predictions, but many studies cannot separate them.
agent_relevance: Our schema should not assume a mechanism. Fresh Look and forgetting a misleading frame are both implementable by clearing context; unconscious work has no LLM analog.

source: Segal (2004) Incubation in insight problem solving; Fresh Look variant, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Fresh Look: simply switching attention away lets a new start happen, with no forgetting and no unconscious work. It predicts no effect of immediate incubation.
numbers: Numbers from Segal's own experiments were not read.
limits: Known only through a secondary summary. Open the original before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Fresh Look is the theory most compatible with a context reset for an LLM: a new attempt without the old reasoning trace is the same idea.

source: Gilhooly et al. (2013) similar vs dissimilar filler tasks, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Crossover design: spatial filler helped verbal divergent thinking more than verbal filler, and verbal filler helped spatial divergent thinking more than spatial filler. Read as support for unconscious work and against forgetting.
numbers: Factorial: filler (anagram vs mental rotation) x target (alternate uses vs mental synthesis), scored for novelty and fluency. Significant incubation effects plus the crossover interaction. Exact N not read.
limits: Ellwood et al. (2009) note that domain-specific fatigue relief gives the same pattern. Review-only source.
agent_relevance: Dissimilar filler may beat similar filler; for an agent, switch to an unrelated subproblem, not a near-copy.

source: Ellwood et al. (2009), as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: A dissimilar interpolated task raised response count in a delayed-incubation fluency test, but the authors say selective fatigue relief fits equally well.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Fluency of uses, not novel uses. Fatigue explanation not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Fatigue has no LLM analog, so any LLM incubation gain would have to come from context change.

source: Gilhooly et al. (2012) immediate vs delayed incubation on alternate uses, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: With standard 'unusual uses' instructions, immediate incubation gave a stronger gain than delayed incubation; both beat control, scored for fluency and novelty.
numbers: Direction only: immediate > delayed > control. Numbers not read.
limits: Cuts against the idea that incubation needs prior fixation.
agent_relevance: A planning pause before work may help as much as one after failure, but see G1.

source: Strick et al. (2011) meta-analysis of unconscious thought, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: A meta-analysis of 92 decision studies gave a small positive effect for a distraction period before deciding.
numbers: g = 0.224. Larger with more options, shorter presentation, shorter incubation, configural mindset.
limits: Later challenged by Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) for small-study bias.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on distraction to improve decisions.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: A meta-analysis and large-scale replication attempt of the unconscious thought advantage (Judgment and Decision Making 10, 1)
finding: The unconscious thought advantage (distraction beats deliberation for complex choices) is mostly small-study bias; the pooled effect vanishes after bias correction.
numbers: 54 articles, 129 comparisons, k = 61 effect sizes. 45 not significant, 12 favoured distraction, 4 favoured deliberation. Random-effects g = 0.15 [0.03, 0.26]. Funnel asymmetry Z = 2.11, p = .04. After trim-and-fill (10 imputed): g = 0.018 [-0.10, 0.14].
limits: Decision making, the cousin of incubation, not insight or divergent tasks. Read through a page summary of the Cambridge page, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Strong reason to distrust claims that off-line mind work improves judgment. G1 and G5 stand.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015) On making the right choice: A meta-analysis and large-scale replication attempt of the unconscious thought advantage (Judgment and Decision Making 10, 1)
finding: A large replication found no distraction advantage.
numbers: N = 399 Dutch students after excluding 24. Within subjects: 58.2% best option after deliberation vs 61.9% after 3-minute word-search distraction, n.s. Fixed 3-minute deliberation 59.4% vs self-paced 56.9% (p = .61). Bayes factor 7.83 favouring the null.
limits: Choice task, not creativity. One population.
agent_relevance: Null results in decision tasks do not settle creativity tasks, but the same fragility applies.

source: Dijksterhuis & Meurs (2006) Where creativity resides, as described in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Immediate incubation (a distraction task after the instructions) gave more creative uses of a brick than conscious thought.
numbers: Numbers not read. Instructions did not ask for unusual uses, so participants may have reported known rare uses rather than new ideas.
limits: Gilhooly's critique: raters score infrequent answers as creative even when they are recalled, not generated.
agent_relevance: Measurement warning: rarity is not creativity. A novelty metric for LLM output must not reward recalled trivia.

source: Ritter et al. (2012b), as described in Ritter & Dijksterhuis (2014) Creativity - the unconscious foundations of the incubation period (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience)
finding: After unconscious thought, people did not generate more creative ideas than after conscious thought, but they chose their best idea better.
numbers: Idea generation similar across conscious and unconscious thought. Selection of the most creative idea better after unconscious thought. Authors argue set-shifting and fatigue cannot explain it because no hints or examples were given.
limits: Single lab. Authors favour the unconscious-thought view.
agent_relevance: Split generation from selection: a break may help choosing more than producing. Selection in our schema is done by code (G5), so this is a caution, not a gain.

source: Smith & Blankenship (1989, 1991) rebus and RAT puzzles with misleading clues; abstract only
finding: Initial misleading clues cause fixation. More puzzles are solved after a delayed retest than an immediate one, and the authors say unconscious work is not needed to explain it.
numbers: Fixation and incubation were both found in every experiment that tested them (abstract wording). Specific rates not read.
limits: Only abstract-level text via a search result. Needs the 1991 Am J Psychol full text (104, 61-87).
agent_relevance: Strongest support for forgetting-fixation: a break helps when there is something to forget. Maps onto clearing a failed reasoning trace before a retry.

source: Smith & Beda (2019) Old problems in new contexts: the context-dependent fixation hypothesis (J Exp Psychol: General)
finding: Experiment 1: fixation on RAT items was induced with misleading words tied to context photos. Resolution of unsolved problems was higher after a delay and higher in a new context.
numbers: N = 146. Incubation main effect F(1,142) = 22.86, p < .001, partial eta2 = .139. Context main effect F(1,142) = 6.18, p = .014, partial eta2 = .042. Interaction F = 1.31, p = .255. Context effect in delayed retest t(145) = 2.28, p = .024, d = .19; immediate t = 1.04, n.s. Initial solve rate 42% vs 60% norm (fixation worked). Delay about 130 s.
limits: Context-by-delay interaction not significant. Delay only about 2 minutes. Undergraduates, one task type.
agent_relevance: A delay and a context change both help release fixation. An LLM retry after a failed attempt probably gains more from a clean context than from time.

source: Smith & Beda (2019) Old problems in new contexts: the context-dependent fixation hypothesis (J Exp Psychol: General)
finding: Experiment 2 replicated Experiment 1 with a longer delay (about 3 minutes) and a better immediate-retest control (one intervening problem).
numbers: About 120 participants (df 119). Interaction F(1,116) = 2.89, p = .092, partial eta2 = .024. Context effect in delayed retest t(119) = 2.43, p = .017, d = .222; immediate t = .36, p = .72, d = .033. Initial solve rate 44% vs 60% norm.
limits: Interaction again not significant. d about .2 is small. Fixation was induced artificially and may overstate real fixation.
agent_relevance: Effects are small even with induced fixation. Expect modest gains from reframing.

source: Baird, Smallwood, Mrazek, Kam, Franklin & Schooler (2012) Inspired by distraction (Psychological Science); abstract and review description
finding: An undemanding filler (0-back) raised creative uses solutions on previously seen problems versus a demanding filler (1-back), rest or no break. The gain appeared only for repeated problems, pointing to incubation rather than warm-up.
numbers: Design: 2 baseline UUT problems (2 min each), then four between-subject conditions, then 4 problems (2 repeated, 2 new). Exact N and effect size not read.
limits: Later larger replication found no difference (next lines).
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'light task beats rest' idea. Shaky.

source: Failed replications of Baird et al. (Smeekens & Kane; Steindorf et al.; Murray et al.), as reported in a 2022 mind-wandering incubation paper
finding: Three later studies did not reproduce the mind-wandering advantage. Probe-caught mind wandering did not predict gains.
numbers: Smeekens & Kane: 3 experiments (0-back, 2-back, reading filler), no correlation of mind wandering with second-attempt gain, no control group. Steindorf et al.: low-load with thought probes, with trivia probes and without probes vs continuous work: no group difference. Murray et al.: larger sample, low-load vs high-load no difference although low-load had more probe-caught mind wandering.
limits: Reported second-hand; exact N not extracted. Probes may disturb the process.
agent_relevance: The 'easy filler beats rest' benefit has not replicated well. Do not build a mind-wandering operator.

source: Mind wandering, mindfulness and the incubation effect (2022 open-access experiment)
finding: A mindfulness filler raised flexibility on the unusual uses task; the mind-wandering-prone filler did not beat control.
numbers: 90 analysed (mindfulness 30, mind-wandering-prone 29, control 31) after dropping 10 who met no impasse and 8 who broke instructions. Diversity of mind wandering predicted flexibility gain in the MW-prone group: r(27) = .40, p = .038.
limits: Small cells. Excluding people with no impasse is sound but rare in older studies. Correlation is exploratory.
agent_relevance: Check that an impasse existed before crediting incubation. Agent analog: score gains only on items that failed first.

source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger & Born (2004) Sleep inspires insight (Nature 427, 352-355); abstract
finding: After 8 hours, more than twice as many subjects found a hidden rule after sleep as after wakefulness.
numbers: More than twice as many gained insight after sleep vs nocturnal or daytime wake. Exact percentages not read here.
limits: Abstract only. One task (number reduction).
agent_relevance: Shows the sleep form of incubation; no LLM analog besides offline consolidation.

source: Lacaux et al. (2021) Sleep onset is a creative sweet spot (Science Advances 7, eabj5866)
finding: A short N1 sleep-onset nap (at least 15 s) tripled the chance to discover a hidden rule; deeper N2 sleep removed the gain.
numbers: N = 103. Rule found: N1 83.33% (20 of 24); Wake 30.61% (15 of 49); N2 14.29% (2 of 14). Fisher p < .001 for N1 vs Wake and N1 vs N2; Wake vs N2 p = .32. 16 people found the rule before the break and were excluded.
limits: Sleep stage not randomized; people fell asleep on their own. One task (mathematical rule discovery).
agent_relevance: Incubation gains depend on the exact state during the break. Nothing like this exists for LLMs. Do not mimic.

source: Sio, Monaghan & Ormerod (2013) Sleep on it, but only if it is difficult (Memory & Cognition); abstract
finding: Sleep helped only on hard RAT items, not easy ones. Authors read this as spreading activation needing a wider search.
numbers: Sleep, wake and no-delay groups; difficulty set by cue-answer association strength. Sleep group solved more difficult problems, no difference on easy ones. Numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Fits the meta-analytic message that incubation helps when the first attempt failed on a hard item.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psychological Review 117, 994-1024); abstract
finding: Explicit-implicit interaction theory: explicit rules and implicit associations run together, are stored redundantly, and their outputs are integrated and iterated. Implemented in CLARION to simulate incubation and insight data.
numbers: Five principles listed in the abstract. Simulation fits not read.
limits: Abstract only. Simulates existing human data. CLARION is a hand-built architecture.
agent_relevance: Closest formal model of incubation: a break lets the implicit system keep running while explicit control is off. An LLM has one system, so the nearest analog is two sampling modes, not two processes.

source: Gupta, Jang, Mednick & Huber (2012) The road not taken: creative solutions require avoidance of high-frequency responses (Psychological Science); abstract via Europe PMC
finding: A semantic-space model of RAT items found correct answers; a frequency-biased model explained both right and wrong responses. People do worse when pulled to high-frequency candidates.
numbers: 48 RAT items under speed pressure. Model details not read.
limits: Paraphrased abstract only.
agent_relevance: High-frequency completions are the default pull of an LLM, so a creative step should discourage them, for example by blocking the first answer.

source: EEG alpha time course in creative ideation (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2014)
finding: Idea generation shows a time course: early common ideas, later new ones. Alpha power rose, fell, then rose before responding; more original ideas went with more right-hemisphere alpha later in the period.
numbers: N = 45 on the Alternative Uses Task. Alpha (10-12 Hz) measured in three equal intervals. The intro also lists stage models: Wallas four stages; Csikszentmihalyi (1996) five stages (preparation, incubation, insight, evaluation, elaboration); Geneplore of Finke et al. (1992) with two repeating phases (generate, explore).
limits: Correlational and does not test incubation. Stage-model descriptions are copied from the paper's introduction.
agent_relevance: Common ideas first, original ideas later: the first LLM sample is the commonest, so originality needs later or blocked samples. Supports generating many and dropping the first.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence)
finding: ChatGPT was tested on 30 verbal insight problems against human solution rates and matched the most probable human score. The paper cites Wallas for the stage model but does not test incubation.
numbers: 15 practice + 15 transfer problems scored 0 or 1; human norms from 20 participants. ChatGPT's score equalled the most probable human outcome; its answer pattern fell within the top 5% of probable human outcomes.
limits: One early model, small human sample, no incubation or stage manipulation. Possible training-data contamination of classic insight puzzles.
agent_relevance: No LLM stage-model test here. Angle B should look for real LLM incubation studies; none were found in this pass.

source: Gilhooly (2016) on Wallas's Intimation sub-stage
finding: Wallas's four stages are widely cited but his Intimation sub-stage (p. 97) is usually ignored. Poincare and Wallas both tied the suddenness and confidence of Illumination to prolonged unconscious work.
numbers: Sadler-Smith (2015) gives an extended discussion of Intimation. No numbers.
limits: Interpretive. The sudden-confidence claim is the part most open to doubt.
agent_relevance: A sudden confident answer is not evidence of correctness (G3: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).
